title: Basic Vocabulary
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Word meanings, word formation, confusable words and context clues

introduction.overview: Vocabulary is the set of words you know and can use correctly. For placement tests, vocabulary questions ask you to give the meaning of a word, pick the right word for a blank, choose the word with the correct spelling or form, or substitute one word for a phrase. A strong vocabulary is built less by memorising long lists and more by learning word parts (prefixes, roots, suffixes), word families, and the context in which words appear.
introduction.placementRelevance: Vocabulary questions are commonly asked in the verbal ability section of company aptitude rounds, in the form of meanings, fill-in-the-blanks, one-word substitutions and confusable-word pairs.
introduction.realWorldContext: The right word makes an email clear and professional. Choosing "advice" instead of "advise", or "effect" instead of "affect", is the kind of detail a reader notices.

learningObjectives: Learn word meanings from context, word parts and word families
Use prefixes and suffixes to form opposites and other word classes
Distinguish commonly confused words (advice/advise, affect/effect, principal/principle)
Build a daily routine for learning and revising new words

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A word family groups words from the same root in different parts of speech: decide (verb), decision (noun), decisive (adjective), decisively (adverb).

coreDefinitions: Prefix: a group of letters added to the beginning of a word that changes its meaning (un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, dis-, re-, mis-).
Suffix: a group of letters added to the end of a word that changes its class or meaning (-tion, -ness, -ous, -ful, -ly).
Root: the core part of a word that carries its basic meaning (bene = good, mal = bad, port = carry).
Context clue: a hint in the sentence that suggests the meaning of an unknown word.
One-word substitution: a single word that replaces a phrase (a person who writes books = author).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: You rarely need to know a word perfectly to answer a vocabulary question. If you recognise a prefix, root or suffix, or you can tell from the sentence whether the word is positive or negative, you can often eliminate three of the four options.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Break an unfamiliar word into parts. "Benevolent": bene = good, vol = wish. So "benevolent" has something to do with wishing good, which means kind and generous. This works for hundreds of words.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Negative prefixes
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: un- (unhappy), in- (inactive), im- before m/p (impossible), il- before l (illegal), ir- before r (irregular), dis- (dislike), non- (nonsense)
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Choose by the first letter of the base word.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Common suffixes
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Suffixes change the part of speech.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Useful roots
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: bene = good (benefit), mal = bad (malfunction), port = carry (transport), dict = say (predict), spect = look (inspect)

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Confusable pairs
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: advice (noun) / advise (verb); affect (verb: to influence) / effect (noun: a result); principal (head or main) / principle (rule); stationary (still) / stationery (paper)
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Rain can affect the harvest; the effect was bad.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: One-word substitution
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: a person who writes books = author; a person who loves mankind = philanthropist; a place where books are kept = library
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: a person who loves mankind → philanthropist

mainNarrative: Start with context. When you meet an unknown word, ask whether the sentence is positive or negative and what kind of word is needed. In "The soldiers were reluctant to fight", reluctant must be a negative word (unwilling), because the soldiers did not want to fight.

Learn the common prefixes and suffixes. In- becomes im- before m and p (impossible, immature), il- before l (illegal) and ir- before r (irregular, irresponsible). Suffixes change the class: decide → decision (noun), danger → dangerous (adjective), quick → quickly (adverb).
Group words in families. Learning decide, decision, decisive and decisively together gives you four forms for the price of one, and these forms are exactly what word-form questions test.

Confusable words are a favourite in tests. Advice is a noun ("good advice") and advise is a verb ("I advise you to study"). Affect is usually a verb meaning to influence and effect is usually a noun meaning a result. Principal means chief or head (the principal of the college) and principle means a rule or belief.

Learn one-word substitutions as small stories: an author writes books, a philanthropist loves mankind and gives to the needy, a librarian looks after books. Revise ten new words a day: write the word, its meaning, a short sentence and one related word.

deepDiveAspects.title: Idioms and phrases
deepDiveAspects.content: Idioms are fixed phrases whose meaning is different from the words alone. "A piece of cake" means something very easy; "to break the ice" means to start a conversation in an awkward situation. Learn idioms with an example sentence.

deepDiveAspects.title: Spelling patterns
deepDiveAspects.content: Many tested words have a double letter: accommodation, committee, necessary, occurrence. Learn them as groups: "accommodation" has double c and double m.

solvedExamples.title: Meaning from word parts
solvedExamples.question: What does "benevolent" mean? (cruel / kind and generous / careless / lazy)
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Use roots: bene = good, vol = wish.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The root bene appears in benefit, beneficial and benefactor, all positive.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Guessing "cruel" because the word looks like "violent".

solvedExamples.title: Confusable words
solvedExamples.question: Choose the correct word: "He gave me good ___ on how to prepare for the interview." (advice / advise)
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Advice is a noun; advise is a verb.

steps.title: Find the class of the word needed
steps.explanation: "Good ___" needs a noun after the adjective good.

steps.title: Match the options
steps.explanation: Advice is the noun; advise is the verb.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The adjective "good" is followed by a noun.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Choosing "advise" because it looks more familiar.

solvedExamples.title: Prefixes
solvedExamples.question: Which prefix gives the opposite of "responsible"? (un- / im- / ir- / dis-)
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Choose the prefix by the first letter of the base word.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.explanation: Before r the negative prefix is ir-.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Negative prefixes follow patterns: im- before m/p, il- before l, ir- before r.

shortcutMethods.title: Parts-and-context method

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Memorise long lists of words with meanings.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: For an unknown word, split it into prefix, root and suffix, decide if the sentence is positive or negative, and eliminate options that do not fit. Learn confusable words in pairs.

rulesForApplication: Positive or negative? Decide this first from the sentence.
in- becomes im-, il- or ir- before m/p, l and r.
Learn word families rather than single words.
Learn confusable pairs together: advice/advise, affect/effect, principal/principle.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing a noun and a verb form
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Check the class of the word needed in the blank.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Thinking that benevolent is like violent.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Learn commonly misspelled words in groups.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: If the sentence is positive in tone, drop options with negative meanings, and vice versa.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Learn words in short daily sessions rather than long weekly lists.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Word parts and context solve most vocabulary questions even when the word is new.

easy.question: The word "abundant" means
easy.explanation: Abundant means existing in large quantities, i.e. plentiful.

easy.question: The word "brief" means
easy.explanation: Brief means lasting a short time or using few words.

easy.question: The word "rapid" means
easy.explanation: Rapid means happening at great speed.

intermediate.question: Which prefix gives the opposite of "responsible"?
intermediate.explanation: Before the letter r the negative prefix is ir-, giving irresponsible.

intermediate.question: Which prefix gives the opposite of "possible"?
intermediate.explanation: Before the letter p the negative prefix is im-, giving impossible.

intermediate.question: The noun form of the verb "decide" is
intermediate.explanation: Decide → decision (noun). Decisive is an adjective.

advanced.question: One word for "a person who loves mankind and gives help to others" is
advanced.explanation: A philanthropist works to improve the lives of others, often by giving money or time.

advanced.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
advanced.explanation: The word has a double c and a double m.

placementStyle.question: The word "benevolent" means
placementStyle.explanation: The root bene means good, so benevolent means well-meaning and kind.

placementStyle.question: The idiom "a piece of cake" means
placementStyle.explanation: The phrase is used for a task that is very easy to do.

placementStyle.question: Choose the correct word: "The school ___ announced the results."
placementStyle.explanation: Principal means the head of a school; principle means a rule. Here the head announces the results.

summaryBullets: Roots: bene, mal, port, dict, spect.

keyTakeaways: Pairs of confusable words need to be learned together.
